name: Stored Credentials
location: Firefox: logins.json (+ key4.db) ; Chrome/Edge: Login Data
purpose: Browser-based password-manager storage holding site credentials a user chose to save, typically protected with Windows DPAPI encryption.
key_fields: Firefox logins.json: hostname, formSubmitURL, encryptedUsername/encryptedPassword, timeCreated, timeLastUsed, timesUsed, timePasswordChanged
Chrome/Edge Login Data (logins table): origin_url, action_url, username_value, password_value (DPAPI-encrypted), date_created, date_last_used
normal_baseline: Stored credentials correspond to known, approved organizational or personal services consistent with the user's role.
anomalies: Stored credentials for services outside the organization's approved application list, especially file-sharing or paste sites
date_last_used timestamps for a credential occurring while the associated account was reported unavailable/offline, suggesting reuse by another party
Credential metadata present but tied to a DPAPI master key or user profile that has been altered, itself worth flagging as possible evasion
anti_forensic_notes: DPAPI ties decryption to the Windows user account — and, for Microsoft cloud accounts on Windows 10/11, to a 44-character randomly generated password rather than the account's actual password — so decrypting real credential values is far easier on a live, logged-in system than from an offline disk image. Metadata (URLs, timestamps, usage counts) remains readable regardless of whether the credential value itself can be decrypted offline.
interpretation: Firefox stores hostname, URL, creation time, last-used time, times-used count, and last-password-change time in JSON even when the credential value itself is encrypted. Chromium browsers store the equivalent in SQLite with origin URL, action URL, username, and created/last-used dates. In both cases, credential metadata is forensically useful even when the encrypted credential value cannot be recovered offline.
